scope.start: 5b: 'Why is this oath necessary?', the purpose of the oath when two hold a garment
scope.end: 7a: 'a certain tenth, not an uncertain tenth', which confirms Rav Chananya's support for Rabba

sections.title: Two Holding a Garment: Why an Oath, and Does It Bind a Thief?
sections.gist: Continuing the Mishnah of two who hold one garment. Three steps: R. Yochanan's takkanah, whether one suspect about money is suspect about oaths, and Abaye's doubtful old loan.

illustration.caption: The Mishnah's case, which this section examines: each claimant holds the garment and claims all of it, the garment is divided, and each swears he has no less than half. R. Yochanan explains the oath as a *takkanat chakhamim* (5b).

children.title: R. Yochanan: An Oath to Stop Grabbing Others' Garments
children.gist: Each claimant already keeps what he holds, so why swear? R. Yochanan: the oath is a rabbinic enactment to deter people from seizing others' garments.

bullets.text: Question: each claimant holds half and ends up with what he holds. Why is an oath needed?
R. Yochanan: the oath is a *takkanat chakhamim*, so that people won't go and seize another's garment and say "It is mine."
This oath is preventive, not evidentiary. It is meant to deter the grab in the first place, or to make the dishonest claimant back down once he stands in court.

The earlier discussion assumed a claimant who is rationalizing and backs down when he must swear outright. This enactment targets someone who grabs knowingly, which raises the question of whether an oath can stop him at all.

children.title: *Migo De'chashid Amamona*: Is One Suspect About Money Suspect About Oaths?
children.gist: The Gemara tests the principle against *modeh be'miktzat*, loans vs. deposits, Rav Huna's paying bailee and three more oaths, and concludes that suspicion about money doesn't carry over to oaths.

chart.caption: Oaths given to someone suspected of lying about money, and why each is accepted
rows: He is evading to buy time and means to repay (Rabba)
"I'll find the thief" or "I'll find it in the marsh"
The deposit was in his house, or in his hand
No excuse remains, so he is disqualified from testifying
Keeps the item and pays for it
"I'm paying for it": people think *lo tachmod* means taking without pay
Rav Nachman, R. Chiya, Rav Sheshet
Denies a debt; storekeeper vs. laborers; the bailee's three oaths
The conclusion: suspicion about money is not suspicion about oaths

children.title: The Principle, and *Modeh Be'miktzat*: Evading, Not Stealing
children.gist: We don't assume that one who lies about money will lie under oath. The Torah's oath for *modeh be'miktzat* seems to prove this, but that debtor may only be buying time.

bullets.text: Objection: if he would seize a garment and lie in court, he should be suspect of swearing falsely too (*migo de'chashid amamona chashid ashvuata*).
Answer: we don't say that. Even a thief treats a false oath as more severe.
Tosafot: a false oath is uniquely grave. The world shook at "*lo tisa*" (Yoma). People are often more careful about ritual matters than about money.
Tosafot's second answer: the oath reaches a person in the middle of his claim, before he has committed himself. A proven *gazlan*, like the shepherd on the previous daf, is past that point.
Proof: if the principle were wrong, the Torah's oath for *modeh be'miktzat* would be pointless, since that defendant is lying about money.
Rejected: there the debtor is evading. Following Rabba, he means to repay everything and admits to part only to buy time.

children.title: Loan vs. Deposit: Rav Chisda, and the Four Bailees
children.gist: Denying a loan is buying time, but denying a deposit is theft. Yet bailees swear too, because even a bailee can be buying time, unless witnesses place the deposit in his house.

bullets.text: Rav Idi bar Avin in the name of Rav Chisda: one who denies a loan and is refuted by witnesses stays fit to testify. One who denies a deposit is disqualified.
The reason: a loan is meant to be spent, so denying it is buying time. A deposit may not be used, so denying it is theft.
Challenge from Rami bar Chama's baraita: all four bailees swear when they deny part of the claim and admit part. Why accept a bailee's oath?
Answer: he may also be buying time, thinking "I'll find the thief and seize it back" or "I'll find it in the marsh and return it."
Then why is one who denies a deposit disqualified? Only where witnesses testify that the deposit was in his house at that moment and he knew it, or that he was holding it in his hand.
In an ordinary case we can't rule out rationalizing, so the oath works. Once witnesses close off that possibility, no excuse is left.

children.title: Rav Huna's Paying Bailee and '*Lo Tachmod*'
children.gist: A bailee who pays yet swears the item isn't with him may tell himself that paying makes it fine, because people think *lo tachmod* applies only to taking without payment.

bullets.text: Rav Huna: a bailee who says the deposit is lost and offers to pay still swears it is not in his possession. Why trust the oath of someone suspected of keeping it?
Answer: he can rationalize: "I'm paying him for it, so I did nothing wrong."
Rav Acha of Difti to Ravina: but taking an item even for payment violates *lo tachmod* (Shemot 20:14).
Answer: most people understand *lo tachmod* as taking without paying, so he may not know he is doing wrong.
A person can break *lo tachmod* and still see himself as honest because he pays. That self-image is what keeps the oath effective.

children.title: Three More Oaths, and the Conclusion: No *Migo*
children.gist: Rav Nachman's *shevuat heset*, R. Chiya's storekeeper and laborers, and Rav Sheshet's three bailee oaths all swear a suspect party, so suspicion about money doesn't disqualify an oath.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman: one who denies a debt entirely takes a *shevuat heset*.
R. Chiya's baraita (see 3a): the storekeeper and the laborers both swear and collect from the employer.
Rav Sheshet: an unpaid bailee who claims the deposit was stolen takes three oaths: he wasn't negligent, he didn't make use of it, and it isn't in his possession.
Conclusion: the court suspects each of these of money wrongdoing and still administers the oath, so we don't say *migo de'chashid amamona chashid ashvuata*.
In the storekeeper case one side is certainly lying, with no obvious excuse. In Rav Sheshet's third oath, if the item is in his closet he is a knowing thief. Yet the oaths stand.

children.title: Abaye: A Doubtful Old Loan, and Why Doubt Stops at Oaths
children.gist: Abaye explains the oaths without trusting a knowing thief: the defendant may be unsure of an old debt owed him. Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi explains why such doubt lets people seize money but not swear.

bullets.text: Abaye: there is no proof. Perhaps the defendant has an old loan owed to him and is taking repayment, not stealing.
Objection: if so, let him take it without an oath, since the oath won't reveal anything.
Revised: he is unsure whether he has an old loan, and holds on to the item just in case.
Objection: if doubt lets him seize property, why won't he swear on the same doubt?
Rav Sheshet son of Rav Idi: people refrain from a doubtful oath but not from doubtful money. Money can be returned; an oath cannot be retracted.
In practice Abaye and the anonymous Gemara cover the same cases. They differ in theory: whether even a knowing thief fears an oath, or whether people almost always find some excuse.

The insight about irreversibility: people allow themselves latitude where a wrong can be undone and are careful where it can't. The lecturer tied this to speech between people and to the season before Rosh Hashanah.

sections.title: R. Zeira: One Seizes the Garment Before the Court
sections.gist: R. Zeira asks whether a seizure in the court's presence counts. Rav Nachman's baraita seems to answer him, but the Gemara reads it two other ways and the question stays open.

children.title: Silent, Then Shouting: Concession or Relying on the Judges?
children.gist: The question is narrowed to one who was silent at first and protested later. Did his silence concede, or did he assume the judges had seen the grab?

bullets.text: R. Zeira asks: both held the garment and one seized all of it in front of the court. What is the halakha?
If the other stayed silent, his silence admits the seizer's claim. If he shouted, what more could he do? Being stronger proves nothing about ownership.
The case in question: he was silent at first and shouted later. Did he concede and then regret it, or was he silent because "the Rabbis saw him grab it from me"?

children.title: Rav Nachman's Baraita: 'In the Possession of Only One'
children.gist: The baraita puts the *burden of proof* on the one not holding. Read literally it would be obvious, so it seems to mean a seizure in court, but the Gemara offers two other cases.

bullets.text: Rav Nachman cites a baraita: both swear and divide only while both are holding. If only one holds the garment, the *burden of proof* is on the claimant.
Read literally, that is obvious. So it must mean that one seized it in the court's presence, which would answer R. Zeira in favor of the one who seized it.
That would be surprising: in a dispute over a found object, with no evidence either way, why should whoever holds it at the moment of the struggle become the one in possession?

chart.caption: Rav Nachman's baraita: the readings the Gemara considers
columns: Why the other must bring proof
rows: No: too obvious to need teaching
Both held; one seized it before the judges
One returned holding it; the other says he rented him his half
He rented to an alleged robber without witnesses?
One holds the garment, the other only its edge
The edge counts for nothing, even for Sumchos

children.title: They Went to Divide and Came Back: 'You Rented It Without Witnesses?'
children.gist: The first deflection: the baraita is about claimants who were told to divide and returned with one holding. The other's story of a rental is implausible.

bullets.text: The case: they came before the court both holding, were told "go divide it", and came back with one of them holding it.
The holder says: "He admitted it to me." The other says: "I rented him my half for money."
We say to the second: until now you called him a robber, and now you rented to him without witnesses? So the one not holding must bring proof.

children.title: Holding Only the Edge: Even Sumchos Concedes
children.gist: The second deflection keeps the baraita literal: one held the garment and the other only its edge, which counts for nothing even according to Sumchos.

bullets.text: Alternatively: one held the garment itself and the other held only its edge.

The baraita's point: Sumchos divides property of uncertain ownership without an oath, yet even he concedes that holding the edge is worth nothing, so the *burden of proof* is on the one holding the edge.

sections.title: Consecrating a Disputed Item: Verbal *Hekdesh*, the Bathhouse and *Safek Bechor*
sections.gist: If a seizure in court holds, does consecrating count as seizing? A disputed bathhouse raises the question in practice. Rav Hamnuna answers from a *safek bechor*, and Rabba replies that a priest who seizes one is removed, a view supported from animal tithe.
sections.continues: On 7a Rav Acha of Difti asks which uncertain animals the tithe baraita means. The bathhouse is then resolved by Rav Nachman's principle: property one cannot recover by legal process cannot be consecrated while it is in another's hands.

children.title: If Seizure Holds: Is Verbal *Hekdesh* Like Seizing?
children.gist: If the court would remove a seized garment, consecrating it is void. If not, a declaration to the Temple might equal seizing, or might fail because the item isn't in his possession.

bullets.text: R. Zeira's question is left unresolved. If a garment seized in court is taken back from the seizer, then consecrating the whole garment is void, since it isn't his.
If the seizer keeps it, what if one of them consecrated the whole garment without seizing it?
For it taking effect: *amirato la'gavoha ki'mesirato la'hedyot*. A declaration to the Most High equals a transfer to an ordinary person, so he is like one who seized it.
Against: he didn't actually seize it. "When a man shall sanctify his house" (Vayikra 27:14): just as his house is in his possession, so too anything he consecrates must be.
If the words count as seizing, the other's silence might be a concession. If the words cannot touch what the other is holding, he has nothing to answer and his silence means nothing.

children.title: The Disputed Bathhouse: The Rabbis Keep Away
children.gist: One of two claimants consecrated a bathhouse that neither possessed. The Rabbis stopped bathing there and sent the question to Rav Chisda.

bullets.text: Two people each claimed a bathhouse that neither possessed. One of them consecrated it.
Rav Chananya, Rav Oshaya and all the Rabbis stopped bathing there, fearing misuse of consecrated property.
Rav Oshaya asked Rabba to put the question to Rav Chisda in Kafri.
The consecration apparently came out of frustration at the deadlock between the claimants.

children.title: Does a Priest Keep a *Safek Bechor* He Seizes? Rav Hamnuna vs. Rabba
children.gist: Rav Hamnuna reads the Teharot mishnah as letting a priest keep a seized uncertain firstborn, so consecration without possession works. Rabba says the priest is removed and the firstborn's sanctity is intrinsic. Rav Chananya supports Rabba from animal tithe.

chart.caption: Rav Hamnuna vs. Rabba on the uncertain firstborn
columns: Why shearing and work are forbidden
rows: His power to keep it gives the animal sanctity even unseized
The consecration takes effect without possession
The court removes it: ownership by force means nothing

children.title: Rav Hamnuna: Kept by the Owner, Yet No Shearing or Work
children.gist: The mishnah leaves an uncertain firstborn with its owner, yet forbids shearing and working it. Rav Hamnuna infers that a priest's power to keep it once seized makes it holy, so the bathhouse consecration works.

bullets.text: In Sura, Rav Hamnuna cites Teharot 4:12: for uncertain firstborns, human or animal, kosher or donkey, the burden of proof is on the claimant. The priest cannot take it.
A baraita adds: shearing and working such an animal are forbidden.
Rav Hamnuna: the mishnah implies that a priest who seized it would keep it. That potential alone makes it holy even unseized. So too the bathhouse consecration takes effect.

Two readings of *hamotzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah* where the doubt is objective: a real ruling that it is the owner's, or a hands-off standstill in which a priest who grabs it is no robber and the owner becomes the claimant.
The owner may wait for a blemish and then eat the animal, but may not treat it as ordinary livestock.

children.title: Rabba: The Priest Is Removed; Sanctity That Comes by Itself
children.gist: Rabba rejects the proof: a priest who seizes is removed, and the ban on shearing and work comes from the firstborn's own intrinsic sanctity, not from anyone's claim to it.

bullets.text: Rabba: no proof. A priest who seizes an uncertain firstborn is removed, since ownership taken by force means nothing. The priest must prove it is a firstborn.
Shearing and work are still forbidden because *kedushah ha'ba'ah me'eleha* is different: a firstborn is holy from birth, not by anyone's act, so the doubt lies in the animal itself.
Money and *issur* run on separate tracks. The animal can be definitively the owner's in monetary law and still be a doubtful firstborn he may not use.
The question underneath: when we rule "the claimant must bring proof" under objective doubt, have we decided ownership, or only declined to disturb the status quo? That is what the tithe proof tests.

children.title: Rav Chananya's Support from *Ma'aser Behemah*
children.gist: Uncertain firstborns enter the tithe pen, which works only if a priest who seizes one is removed. Abaye first limits the proof to nine animals plus one, then retracts, because a doubtful animal can't be tithed.

children.title: Uncertain Firstborns Enter the Pen
children.gist: If a priest could keep an uncertain firstborn he seized, tithing it would exempt the owner's flock with the priest's property.

bullets.text: Rav Chananya cites a baraita: uncertain firstborns enter the pen to be tithed together with the other young animals.
If a priest who seized one could keep it, the owner would be exempting his own flock with the priest's property.
The lecturer explains these as lambs given to redeem a donkey that may be a firstborn, and describes the pen: the animals pass through one by one and every tenth is holy.

children.title: Abaye: Only Nine Plus One, So Either Way He's Covered
children.gist: Abaye deflects the proof: with exactly nine animals plus the uncertain one, the owner either tithes properly or owes nothing.

bullets.text: Abaye: no support. The case is an owner with nine animals plus the uncertain one.
If it isn't a firstborn, it is his: ten animals, and he tithes properly. If it is a firstborn, it is the priest's, and nine animals aren't subject to tithe.
With more animals the reasoning fails: if the uncertain animal came out tenth, he might be exempting himself with the priest's property.

children.title: Abaye Retracts: The Animal That Jumped Back, and a Tally Fit to Reach Ten
children.gist: If a counted animal jumps back into the pen, all are exempt, even though an either-way argument, backed by Rava's *minyan ha'ra'uy*, would let the count go on.

bullets.text: Abaye: I was wrong; an uncertain firstborn is not subject to tithe. Mishnah (Bekhorot 58b): if a counted animal jumps back among the uncounted, all in the pen are exempt.
If doubt could be tithed, he should keep counting. Either the next ten obligate him and he tithes properly, or one of them was already counted and the other nine are exempt anyway.
Rava: *minyan ha'ra'uy*, a tally fit to reach ten, exempts the animals counted even if it is cut short, for example when one dies and only nine remain.

children.title: 'A Certain Tenth, Not an Uncertain Tenth'
children.gist: The Torah requires a certain tenth, so doubt can't be tithed even when either way would work. The baraita's animals must belong to the owner outright, which proves that a priest who seizes one is removed.

bullets.text: Why, then, is the flock exempt? "The tenth shall be holy" (Vayikra 27:32): a certain tenth, not an uncertain one.
So an animal that is uncertain can't be tithed even where either way covers it. The baraita's uncertain animals must be the owner's outright, which proves that a priest who seizes one is removed.
*Hamotzi me'chavero alav ha'ra'ayah* is thus a definitive ruling of ownership, not a standstill waiting to see who grabs first.

children.continues: On 7a Rav Acha of Difti asks which uncertain animals the baraita means, since an uncertain firstborn is already holy.

key_terms.sense: suspicion about money extending to oaths
key_terms.definition: The proposed inference that one suspected of dishonesty in money matters is also suspect of swearing falsely. The accepted rule is that we do not draw this inference, since people fear a false oath more than monetary wrongdoing.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Gemara tests the rule against a series of oaths given to people suspected of lying about money, and concludes that suspicion about money does not disqualify an oath.

key_terms.definition: A defendant who admits part of a monetary claim and denies the rest; the Torah obligates him to take an oath on the part he denies.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The Torah's oath for a partial admitter seems to prove that one lying about money can swear. The Gemara deflects this: he is only buying time to repay.

key_terms.sense: burden of proof on the claimant
key_terms.definition: The principle that one who seeks to take property from its current possessor must bring proof; without it, the property stays where it is.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Applied to one holding a garment and to an uncertain firstborn; the daf asks whether under objective doubt it decides ownership or merely leaves things as they are, and concludes that it decides ownership.

key_terms.sense: verbal consecration as an act of transfer
key_terms.definition: The rule that declaring property consecrated to the Temple is as effective as a formal act of acquisition in an ordinary transfer between people.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Suggested as a reason why consecrating a disputed garment might count as seizing it, against the requirement that consecrated property be in one's possession.

key_terms.sense: an animal or child of uncertain firstborn status
key_terms.definition: A human or animal whose status as a firstborn is in doubt, so that the priest's claim to it cannot be proven while the prohibitions of a firstborn may still apply.
key_terms.on_this_daf: The owner keeps it without proof from the priest, yet may not shear or work it; Rav Hamnuna and Rabba dispute whether a priest who seizes it keeps it.

key_terms.definition: Sanctity that takes effect on its own, such as a firstborn animal's holiness from birth, rather than through a person's act of consecration.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rabba's reason why an uncertain firstborn may not be sheared or worked even though a priest who seizes it is removed.

key_terms.definition: The tithe of cattle and sheep: the year's young are passed one by one under a rod, and every tenth is holy.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rav Chananya proves from uncertain firstborns entering the tithe pen that a priest who seizes one is removed.

key_terms.sense: a tally fit to reach ten in tithing
key_terms.definition: Animals counted for the animal tithe while the count could still reach ten are exempt from future tithing, even if the count is cut short.
key_terms.on_this_daf: Rava's principle makes an either-way argument for continuing to count after an animal jumps back, which fails only because the Torah requires a certain tenth.

judgment_calls: The migo discussion (s3) and Abaye's doubtful old loan (s8) are kept as children of one section on the oath's purpose; each could stand as its own top-level section, but both answer the same question R. Yochanan's takkanah raises: can an oath bind someone grabbing property?

The consecration inquiry (s15) could sit under R. Zeira's question (s9), since it is phrased 'if you say' off his question. It was grouped instead with the bathhouse and the firstborn, because the rest of the daf answers the consecration question and never returns to the seizure.
The animal-tithe discussion (s20) is nested under the Rav Hamnuna vs. Rabba debate rather than made top-level, because it is offered solely as support for Rabba. That makes it four levels deep.
Rav Nachman's baraita (s11) carries its own bullets for the proposed proof, with the two deflections as children, rather than being three sibling sections.
The Gemara's 'certain tenth' conclusion (s24) is its own section rather than the last bullet of s23, because it is what finally settles the tithe proof for Rabba.
coverage_notes: The whole scope is covered by the shiur; no section is flagged as Gemara text only.
The essay and segmentation name 'Rabbi Chanina' (at the bathhouse, and as the source of the tithe proof); the text has Rav Chananya in both places. Followed the text.

The essay says the other claimant in the returned-garment case said the holder 'agreed to buy his half' and that he 'sold' it; the text says he claims he rented half the garment to him. Followed the text.

The segmentation reads the Teharot mishnah as 'even if the priest grabs it, the owner can take it back'; in the text Rav Hamnuna reads the mishnah as letting a priest who seized it keep it, and only Rabba holds that he is removed. Followed the text.
The essay attributes the theory that the priest's potential seizure creates sanctity to 'the gemara'; the text attributes it to Rav Hamnuna. Followed the text.
The essay speaks of a 'shomeret' who denies a debt entirely; the text has Rav Nachman's ruling on anyone who denies a debt entirely. Followed the text.

The essay identifies the uncertain animals in the tithe baraita as redemption lambs for an uncertain firstborn donkey. The text in scope calls them uncertain firstborns; the Gemara's clarification comes on 7a.2, outside scope. The lecturer's identification is kept as a shiur bullet.
Material from 7a.2 onward (Rav Acha of Difti's question, Rav Nachman's ruling that resolves the bathhouse) is outside scope; it is mentioned only in 'continues'.
